title: Postpartum haemorrhage: the surgical ladder
subtitle: Drugs, balloon, sutures, ligation, hysterectomy

sources.org: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG)
sources.title: Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage (Green-top Guideline No. 52; BJOG 2017;124:e106-e149)

sources.org: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO)
sources.title: FIGO recommendations on the management of postpartum hemorrhage 2022 (Int J Gynecol Obstet 2022)
WHO recommendation on tranexamic acid for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage

red_flags.text: Blood loss above 1000 mL with continuing bleeding, or any loss with clinical shock: major PPH.
Tachycardia, pallor, agitation and falling urine output. Pregnant women compensate well and become hypotensive late.
Pain out of proportion, a high-riding uterus or an abnormal contour: uterine rupture or a broad ligament haematoma.
Bleeding that does not clot, oozing from cannula sites: coagulopathy, including amniotic fluid embolism or abruption.
Previous caesarean with placenta praevia: high risk of placenta accreta spectrum and massive haemorrhage.

do_now.text: Call for help: senior midwife, senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, haematology and the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol. Assign a scribe and measure blood loss.
Rub up a contraction (bimanual compression if needed), empty the bladder, and check that the placenta is complete. Think of the four Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin.
Uterotonics in sequence per RCOG GTG 52: oxytocin and ergometrine (unless hypertensive), oxytocin infusion, then carboprost and misoprostol. Use the doses in the local protocol derived from GTG 52.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously as soon as possible and within three hours of birth; a second 1 g dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.
Two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, coagulation and fibrinogen; transfuse to the major haemorrhage protocol.

assess.text: Quantify blood loss by weighing or measuring rather than estimating; visual estimates underestimate.
Examine the genital tract under good light and anaesthesia for trauma: cervical, vaginal and perineal tears.
Trend heart rate, blood pressure, shock index and urine output.

investigate.text: Full blood count, coagulation screen, fibrinogen, crossmatch, and point-of-care viscoelastic testing where available.
Venous or arterial gas with lactate and calcium.
Ultrasound for retained products if the cause is unclear and the woman is stable enough.

resuscitate.text: Red cells, plasma and platelets per the major haemorrhage protocol; replace fibrinogen early, guided by levels or viscoelastic tests.
Keep warm, maintain calcium, and use cell salvage where available.
Non-pneumatic anti-shock garment as a temporising measure during transfer in low-resource settings.

definitive.text: Move to surgery sooner rather than later when pharmacological measures fail. Repair genital tract trauma and remove retained tissue first if they are the cause.
Intrauterine balloon tamponade is the first-line surgical step for atony when uterotonics fail.
At laparotomy: haemostatic compression (brace) sutures such as B-Lynch, then bilateral uterine artery ligation, then internal iliac artery ligation by a surgeon experienced in it.
Selective arterial embolisation by interventional radiology in a stable woman where it is immediately available.
Hysterectomy sooner rather than later, particularly with placenta accreta or uterine rupture. A second experienced consultant should be involved in the decision where possible.

escalate.text: Consultant obstetrician and consultant anaesthetist present for major PPH.
Interventional radiology and a vascular or gynae-oncology surgeon early when accreta is known or suspected.
Critical care after major haemorrhage, hysterectomy or massive transfusion.

notes: The ladder is climbed quickly. A woman who has lost two litres while each rung is tried for half an hour has been managed too slowly.
Tone is the commonest cause, but trauma is the commonest missed cause. Examine the genital tract properly.
A hysterectomy done in time is a life saved. One done after the fourth litre of transfusion is a gamble.
